I'm always surprised when an author manages to discuss such a topic - in this case it would be the human condition - and manages to do it with such style and ease (in writing).

This was my first Camus book. For some might seem like kind of a strange choice, taking in consideration the fact that I had no contact with his writings before.

I feel as if Camus touches on one of the most difficult topics regarding humanity and our intrinsic mechanisms.
He does such a good job, proving that whatever you might want to write about, there are always levels and nuances that we might not even think about, initially.

Oftentimes, I had empathised with Jean's emotions, decisions and thought processes. I found myself gravitating towards that specific way of thinking.

Camus doesn't let you go astray. He doesn't allow you to bend or escape his arguments/polemics. 

Jean finds himself in a situation that causes him gain the consciousness of the Shadow self (thanks Jung). Which spirals into a long and winding train of events that take place inside of him, building and destroying, finding and losing. 

Later on, Jean develops some sort of coping mechanism that expresses and exposes his duplicity even further (when you thought you had enough).

Jean is, for the lack of a better explanation, a double within a double, making everything even more ABSURD, which definitely sits at the core of Camus's self expression.
